title: Bold Conjectures, Volume II: Essays Across Physics
author: Logan Chipkin (editor)
openingText: If we really do live in a quantum multiverse, then where does gravity fit into that picture? How does quantum theory solve the problem of time? How can the world be truly local, despite quantum theory’s notoriously bizarre properties? Can we ever settle the debate over whether entropy is subjective or objective? What is the relationship between probability and fundamental reality?
about:
Bold Conjectures, Volume II gathers thirteen essays by fourteen physicists and philosophers of physics, edited by Logan Chipkin. Each essay either explains a development at the edge of current research or corrects an idea that popular accounts usually get wrong. The preface states the questions: where gravity fits in a quantum multiverse, how quantum theory bears on the problem of time, how the world can be local despite quantum strangeness, whether entropy is subjective, and how probability relates to reality.

Several essays draw on the many-worlds and constructor-theory research associated with David Deutsch and Oxford. Sam Kuypers asks what many worlds means for gravity. Chiara Marletto and Vlatko Vedral recast quantum physics and general relativity as 'superinformation'. Antonia Weber and Giuseppe Di Pietra describe experiments that could test whether gravity, or a living system, is non-classical. Charles Alexandre Bédard gives a local account of Bell's theorem, and David Wallace argues that probability cannot be understood without many-worlds. Others deal with the subjectivity of entropy (Maria Violaris), string theory's history (Aditya Iyer), time (Simone Rijavec), entanglement witnesses (Mia Stamatova), effective field theory (Abdullah Afzal and Hassaan Saleem) and gravity without absolute space or time (Julian Barbour).

The essays are written for non-specialists but do not avoid equations, figures or references. Each stands alone. Read them in any order, for a picture of what physicists in this tradition think is unsettled.

whyItMatters.title: Unsettled questions in fundamental physics
whyItMatters.body:
The book deals with questions that textbooks often present as closed or ignore: the measurement problem, the meaning of probability, whether entropy depends on an observer, and how to reconcile quantum theory with gravity. Each essay states a position and argues for it.

Today: Popular science tends to report results; these essays explain the arguments behind them.

whyItMatters.title: Proposals that can be tested
whyItMatters.body:
Several contributors describe experiments designed to settle a philosophical question, such as entangling two masses through gravity alone or using a quantum probe to detect non-classical behaviour in photosynthesis. The book follows how a conceptual argument becomes a laboratory proposal.

Today: Table-top tests of quantum gravity are an active area of experimental work.

whyItMatters.title: Many-worlds taken seriously
whyItMatters.body:
Many essays assume, defend or test the Everett interpretation. Violaris asks whether its rival, the Copenhagen interpretation, can itself be tested, and Wallace argues that probability is only intelligible within many-worlds.

Today: Physicists remain divided about what quantum theory says exists, and this book sets out one side in detail.

angleCards.title: The gravity thread
angleCards.text: Read the essays by Kuypers, Marletto and Vedral, Weber, Iyer and Barbour together. Compare how each approaches reconciling gravity with quantum theory.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to compare how the essays in Bold Conjectures, Volume II approach the relationship between gravity and quantum theory.

angleCards.title: Many-worlds and probability
angleCards.text: Follow Violaris on testing Copenhagen, Bédard on locality and Wallace on probability. Note what each argument requires you to accept about the multiverse.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow the arguments about the many-worlds interpretation in Bold Conjectures, Volume II, especially on testability, locality and probability.

angleCards.title: From idea to experiment
angleCards.text: Focus on Di Pietra's photon witness in biology, Weber's tests of gravity and Stamatova's thermodynamic witnesses. Ask what result would count against each claim.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to understand the experimental proposals in Bold Conjectures, Volume II and what outcomes would refute the claims they test.

angleCards.title: Read for the explanation
angleCards.text: Skip the equations on a first pass and follow the argument in words. Return to the mathematics only where the prose depends on it.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to understand the central argument of each essay in Bold Conjectures, Volume II without working through every equation.

cast.name: Logan Chipkin
cast.description: President and Cofounder of Conjecture Institute. He wrote the preface and edits the Bold Conjectures series; Volume I collected interviews of David Deutsch, and this volume turns to original essays.

cast.name: Sam Kuypers
cast.description: Researcher at Conjecture Institute working on the foundations of quantum theory, the many-worlds theory, the nature of time and the physics of time travel.

cast.name: Maria Violaris
cast.role: ESSAYS 2 AND 3, ON ENTROPY AND COPENHAGEN
cast.description: Quantum physicist and science communicator working on thermodynamics, quantum physics and constructor theory. She wrote both essays for an Oxford philosophy of physics course in 2021 and introduces them in 'A Note on These Essays'.

cast.name: Charles Alexandre Bédard
cast.description: Researcher at École de technologie supérieure (ETS) working on the foundations of quantum mechanics, locality and algorithmic information theory.

cast.name: Giuseppe Di Pietra
cast.description: Researcher at the University of Oxford working on quantum biology, non-classicality and hybrid quantum-classical systems.

cast.name: Chiara Marletto and Vlatko Vedral
cast.description: Researchers at the Clarendon Laboratory, University of Oxford. Marletto works on constructor theory, quantum information and testing the quantum nature of gravity; Vedral on quantum information theory, the foundations of quantum mechanics and the relationship between information and physics.

cast.name: Antonia Weber
cast.role: ESSAY 7 — TESTS OF THE NATURE OF GRAVITY
cast.description: Physicist at the University of Oxford working on quantum gravity, testing the nature of gravity and quantum cosmology.

cast.name: Aditya Iyer
cast.description: Visiting Researcher at the University of Oxford and CEO and co-founder of Allos AI, working on quantum gravity signatures, quantum information theory and cosmology.

cast.name: Simone Rijavec
cast.role: ESSAY 9 — THE QUANTUM SOLUTION TO AN ANCIENT PROBLEM
cast.description: Researcher at Tel Aviv University working on the quantum nature of time.

cast.name: David Wallace
cast.description: Philosopher and physicist at the University of Pittsburgh, working on many-worlds quantum theory, probability in physics and emergence.

cast.name: Mia Stamatova
cast.description: Researcher at the University of Oxford working on quantum thermodynamics and spatiotemporal entanglement.

cast.name: Abdullah Afzal and Hassaan Saleem
cast.description: Theoretical physicists: Afzal at the School of Physics and Astronomy, University of Southampton (quantum field theory, foundations of physics), and Saleem at the University at Albany (string theory, supersymmetry).

cast.name: Julian Barbour
cast.description: Independent theoretical physicist whose research addresses the nature of time, quantum gravity and the relational reformulation of dynamics. His essay is an expanded version of a 2025 talk for the Time in Physics International Workshop.
